opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most interesting shifts happening right now. For a long time, the conversation around open models was framed as, "Can they catch up to the frontier?" Benchmarks, leaderboards, how many months behind GPT or Claude are they. Agents like OpenClaw change the economics of that question in a really fundamental way.

When you're chatting with a model, you send a message, you get a response, maybe a few thousand tokens. When you run an agent, it might go off for twenty minutes, call tools hundreds of times, read files, browse, retry things that failed. You're suddenly consuming orders of magnitude more tokens per task. At that scale the price per token stops being a rounding error and becomes the thing that determines whether the product is viable at all. People who were happy paying for a frontier API for chat are now looking at their bills and saying, "Wait, I'm spending how much for this thing to reorganize my inbox?"

So there's a real pull toward models that are good enough and dramatically cheaper. A lot of agentic work isn't hard reasoning at every step. It's reading output, deciding the next tool call, formatting something. You don't need the absolute best model for every one of those steps. That's where open models, especially the strong Chinese releases like Qwen, DeepSeek, Kimi, and GLM, have found a natural home. They're cheap to serve, you can run them on your own hardware or pick from many inference providers, and they're increasingly trained specifically for tool use and long-horizon behavior.

The other piece is control. If you're running an always-on personal agent with access to your email, files, and accounts, a lot of people are uncomfortable sending all of that through a closed API they don't control. Running locally or on infrastructure you trust is appealing for privacy and also reliability. You don't want your agent to break because a provider changed a model version or a rate limit.

Where I'd add nuance is that this doesn't mean the frontier labs lose. What I expect is a kind of routing world: the hardest planning and the moments where a mistake is costly go to the best closed model, while the bulk of the cheap, repetitive token volume goes to open models. Agents make the total token pie so much bigger that both sides can grow.

For the American open model ecosystem specifically, this is a bit of a wake-up call. The demand is clearly there, and right now a lot of it is being met by Chinese open-weight models. If we care about having strong, open, American-built models that developers actually choose for these agent workloads, this is exactly the moment to invest, because agents are where open model adoption gets locked in.

r001.rationale: The response says token prices determine whether an agent product is viable, but does not state that agent products emerge wherever a viable price band exists.

r002.rationale: It describes demand for cheaper models and their suitability for agent workloads, but does not clearly say low cost makes people more willing to experiment with open models.

r003.rationale: It predicts growing agent token use and open-model adoption, but does not say the kind of agent OpenClaw represents will persist beyond individual products’ popularity.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that agents change the shape of demand for models. When you're chatting with a model, you send one message and read one answer, so you're pretty willing to pay for the very best model on every call. When something like OpenClaw is running, it's making hundreds or thousands of calls in a loop: reading files, planning, checking its own work, retrying. Most of those calls are not hard. They're routing decisions, formatting, summarizing a tool output. If you pay frontier prices for all of them, the economics break fast, and that's exactly where cheap open models slot in.

So the pattern I see emerging is a kind of tiering. You might keep a closed frontier model for the small number of steps that actually require deep reasoning, and then push the bulk of the volume onto something open that's fast, cheap, and good enough. And "good enough" has moved a lot. The gap between the best open models and the best closed models on the kinds of tasks agents do most often is much smaller than it was two years ago, especially when you can fine-tune or at least prompt the open model for a narrow slice of the workflow.

There are a couple of other things pushing this. One is control. If you're running an agent that touches your codebase or your customers' data, having weights you can host yourself, inspect, and pin to a version is really valuable. Agents are already hard to make reliable, and a provider silently updating the model underneath you makes that worse. Open weights give you stability. The second is latency and local execution. A lot of agent steps don't need to leave the machine, and small open models running on a laptop or a modest GPU are now quite capable.

The part I'd push back on a little is the idea that this is purely a race to the bottom on price. Cheap matters, but what people really want is cheap and predictable. The open models that win in the agent era are going to be the ones with solid tool calling, strong instruction following over long contexts, and behavior that doesn't drift. That's less glamorous than topping a benchmark, but it's what actually determines whether someone trusts your model inside a loop that runs unsupervised for an hour.

And frankly, the companies releasing open models are starting to understand that agents are the distribution channel. If OpenClaw or a similar framework defaults to your model for the routine steps, you get enormous usage and feedback, even if you don't capture most of the revenue directly. So I'd expect the pressure to release capable, inexpensive open models to keep increasing as these agents become normal infrastructure rather than demos.

r001.rationale: The response explains that low-cost models fit the high call volume of agents, but does not state that agent products emerge wherever a viable price band exists.

r002.rationale: It says cheap models make high-volume agent use economically viable, but does not say their low cost makes people more willing to experiment with them.

r003.rationale: It predicts agents will become “normal infrastructure rather than demos,” conveying that this kind of agent will persist beyond the popularity of individual products.

astra-6.text:
I think agents make the demand for inexpensive open models much more concrete. If you’re chatting with a model, you might send a handful of messages and then stop. With an agent, one request can turn into dozens of model calls: it looks something up, reads the result, tries an action, encounters an error, and tries again. The cost of that whole loop starts to matter a lot.

And a lot of those individual steps don’t necessarily require the most capable model. You might want a really strong model to make the plan or handle a difficult decision, but a cheaper model can do much of the execution. The question becomes: what’s the cheapest system that reliably completes the task? A cheap model that keeps failing and retrying can actually be more expensive.

Open models are attractive because you have more control over that equation. You can choose where to run them, optimize them for your workload, and potentially keep sensitive information within your own infrastructure. That doesn’t mean running an open model is automatically cheaper—there’s real operational work involved—but it gives people options.

So as something like OpenClaw becomes popular, I’d expect more interest in models that are inexpensive and dependable at tool use. You don’t need every call to be brilliant. You need the entire process to work, at a cost that makes it useful to run repeatedly.

r001.rationale: The response says agent costs matter and asks what system can complete a task cheaply, but does not state that agent products emerge wherever a viable price band exists.

r002.rationale: It describes open models as giving people cost and infrastructure options, but does not explain that low cost makes people more willing to experiment with them.

r003.rationale: It predicts increased interest in inexpensive, dependable tool-use models as OpenClaw becomes popular, but does not say that this kind of agent will persist beyond individual products’ popularity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think agents make the demand for inexpensive open models much more concrete. When you’re chatting with a model, you might send a few messages and wait for an answer. An agent can keep working: it calls tools, reads the results, tries something else, and repeats. That can consume a lot of tokens, so the cost of inference becomes a much bigger part of whether the product makes sense.

And a lot of those steps don’t necessarily need the most capable model. You might want a strong model to make the plan or handle a difficult decision, and a cheaper model to do the routine work. That creates demand for models that are inexpensive but still reliable at following instructions and using tools.

Open models give developers more control over that tradeoff. They can choose where to run them, optimize them for their workload, and decide what data leaves their infrastructure. But open weights don’t automatically mean cheap inference—you still have to operate the model efficiently. The interesting metric is really cost per successfully completed task. If a cheaper model gets stuck in a loop or needs ten retries, the savings can disappear.

r002.rationale: It describes demand for inexpensive models and their practical advantages, but does not say lower cost makes people more willing to experiment with them.

r003.rationale: It discusses how agents work but makes no prediction that this kind of agent will persist beyond the popularity of individual products.
